title: Episode 2 (lines 354–548)

teacherSummary.text: The Guard brings in Antigone, caught performing the rites again. She admits the act and defends it: Creon's edict cannot override the unwritten laws of the gods. Creon condemns her. Ismene tries to share the blame; Antigone refuses her. Creon orders both sisters held.

context.history: Antigone appeals to divine, unwritten law; Creon to the authority of the State. Hegel reads the play as a collision of two powers: Antigone reverences the ties of blood and the gods below, while Creon recognizes Zeus as the power of public life (Hegel, 1838/1920, sec. "The Concrete Development of Dramatic Poetry and its Types").

significance: Two stubborn wills meet. Creon's fear that "I am woman, she the man" (lines 449–450) shows that his anger is also about gender and power.
